questions.title: Enum Declaration
questions.description: Which keyword is used to define an enumeration type in Java?
options: enum
enumeration
enumerator
define
questions.explanation: Enums in Java are declared using the 'enum' keyword: enum Day { MONDAY, TUESDAY, ... }. Java enums are more powerful than in most other languages — they are full-fledged classes that can have fields, methods, and constructors.
hints: This keyword is shorter than 'enumeration'
Java enums are full-featured reference types

questions.title: Enum Values Method
questions.description: What does the Day.values() method return, given: enum Day { MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI, SAT, SUN }?
options: A String array containing the enum constant names
An array of all Day constants in the order they were declared
A List of Day constants sorted alphabetically
The number of enum constants (7)
questions.explanation: Day.values() returns an array of all Day enum constants in the order they were declared: [MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI, SAT, SUN]. The values() method is implicitly added by the compiler to every enum class. It is commonly used to iterate over all enum constants.
hints: This method returns an array, not a count
The order matches the declaration order in the enum definition

questions.title: Enum with Fields
questions.description: What is the output of the following Java code?
options: MEDIUM
M
A compilation error — enums cannot have fields
Size.MEDIUM
questions.explanation: Java enums can have fields, constructors, and methods. Each enum constant is created with the constructor argument specified in parentheses: MEDIUM("M") calls the constructor Size("M") which sets code to "M". getCode() returns this value, so Size.MEDIUM.getCode() returns "M". Enum constructors are implicitly private.
hints: Enum constants can pass arguments to their constructor
Look at what value is passed to MEDIUM in the enum definition

questions.title: Switch with Enum
questions.description: Can enums be used in switch statements in Java?
options: No, enums cannot be used in switch statements
Yes, enums work perfectly in switch statements
Yes, but only if the enum is declared inside the class
No, switch only works with primitives and strings
questions.explanation: Enums can be used in switch statements. The case labels use the unqualified enum constant names (e.g., case MONDAY: instead of case Day.MONDAY:). The compiler ensures all enum constants are handled (or you need a default branch). This is one of the most common and elegant uses of enums.
hints: Switch cases use the enum constant name without the enum type prefix
Enums were designed to work well with switch statements

questions.title: What is a Record?
questions.description: What is a Java Record (introduced in Java 16)?
options: A class that saves its state to a database
A transparent carrier of immutable data with automatically generated constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString
A file format for storing Java objects
A type of enum that can have mutable fields
questions.explanation: A record is a special kind of class that acts as a transparent carrier for immutable data. Declaring 'record Point(int x, int y) { }' automatically generates: a canonical constructor, accessor methods (x(), y()), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Records are implicitly final and cannot be extended. The components are private final fields.
hints: Records eliminate boilerplate for simple data carriers
Think of them as 'data classes' with auto-generated methods

questions.title: Nested Class Types
questions.description: Which of the following is a type of nested class in Java?
options: Static nested class, inner class (non-static), local class, anonymous class
Public nested class, private nested class, abstract nested class
Static inner class, dynamic inner class, inherited class
Only static nested classes exist in Java
questions.explanation: Java has four types of nested classes: (1) Static nested classes — declared static inside another class; (2) Inner classes (non-static nested) — have access to the enclosing instance; (3) Local classes — defined inside a method body; (4) Anonymous classes — defined and instantiated in a single expression, often used for event handlers or functional interfaces.
hints: Two types are static/non-static at the class level
The other two are defined inside methods

questions.title: Enum with Abstract Method
questions.description: What is the output of the following Java code?
options: A compilation error — enums cannot have abstract methods
ADD SUBTRACT
questions.explanation: Enums can declare abstract methods that each enum constant implements individually. This is a powerful pattern for implementing type-safe behavior without switch statements. ADD implements apply() as addition (5+3=8), SUBTRACT implements it as subtraction (5-3=2). Each constant gets its own behavior. This is essentially the Strategy pattern implemented with enums.
hints: Each enum constant provides its own implementation of the abstract method
ADD adds, SUBTRACT subtracts

questions.title: Anonymous Class Example
questions.description: What is the output of the following Java code?
options: Hello, Alice
A compilation error — anonymous classes cannot implement interfaces
Greeter@1a2b3c
Alice
questions.explanation: This code creates an anonymous class that implements the Greeter interface and overrides its greet() method. Anonymous classes are defined and instantiated in one expression: 'new Interface() { ... }'. They are commonly used for event listeners, callbacks, and, before Java 8, for implementing functional interfaces. In modern Java, this would typically be written as a lambda: Greeter g = name -> "Hello, " + name.
hints: Anonymous classes define the implementation inline
The syntax is: new InterfaceName() { method implementations }

questions.title: Static Nested Class Access
questions.description: How do you create an instance of a static nested class?
options: Outer.Nested n = new Outer.Nested();
Outer.Nested n = new Outer().new Nested();
Outer.Nested n = Outer.new Nested();
Nested n = new Nested();
questions.explanation: Static nested classes are instantiated using the enclosing class name: new Outer.Nested(). They do not require an instance of the outer class because they are static. A static nested class can access only static members of the outer class (staticMsg in this case). Non-static inner classes would require an outer instance: new Outer().new Inner().
hints: Static nested classes are like top-level classes grouped under a parent name
No outer instance is needed — only the outer class name

questions.title: Inner Class Has Outer Reference
questions.description: What is true about non-static inner classes in Java?
options: They cannot access private members of the outer class
They hold an implicit reference to the enclosing outer class instance
They cannot be instantiated at all
They are rarely used in Java
questions.explanation: Non-static inner classes hold an implicit reference to the enclosing instance (Outer.this). This allows them to access all members of the outer class, including private ones. To create an inner class instance, you need an outer class instance: new Outer().new Inner(). This is useful for classes that logically belong to an enclosing instance, like iterators or views.
hints: The inner class is 'attached' to an outer class instance
It uses Outer.this to refer to the enclosing instance

questions.title: Local Class
questions.description: Where can a local class be defined in Java?
options: Only at the top level of a file, outside all classes
Inside a method body, constructor, or initializer block
Inside an interface only
Local classes cannot be defined in Java
questions.explanation: Local classes are defined inside a method body, constructor, or initializer block. They are scoped to that block and cannot be accessed outside it. Local classes can access effectively final local variables and all members of the enclosing class. They are useful when you need a simple, one-off class within a single method.
hints: The name 'local' suggests scope limited to a code block
They are defined where local variables are defined — inside methods

questions.title: Record Canonical Constructor
questions.description: What does the automatically generated constructor for the following record look like?
options: public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
public Point() { this.x = 0; this.y = 0; }
public Point(int x, int y) { }
No constructor is generated
questions.explanation: The compiler automatically generates the canonical constructor: a constructor with exactly the same parameters as the record components, assigning each to the corresponding private final field. You can also define a compact constructor (without parameters) for validation or normalization without repeating the assignment.
hints: The generated constructor assigns each parameter to the corresponding field
The fields are private final and match the component names

questions.title: Enum Singleton Pattern
questions.description: Why is an enum considered the best way to implement the Singleton pattern in Java?
options: Because enum constants are compiled faster than classes
Because enum singletons provide serialization safety and are immune to reflection attacks
Because enums can only be instantiated once in the JVM memory
Because enum constructors can be public
questions.explanation: Enum singletons are the recommended approach per Joshua Bloch's Effective Java because: (1) They are inherently serialization-safe — the JVM ensures only one instance exists even after deserialization. (2) They are immune to reflection attacks (reflection cannot create additional enum instances). (3) They provide thread-safety for free. (4) The pattern is concise: public enum Singleton { INSTANCE }.
hints: This pattern protects against two specific JVM-level attacks
No multi-threading boilerplate is needed

questions.title: Record with Validation
questions.description: How can you add validation to a Java Record's constructor?
options: This cannot be done — records cannot have custom constructors
Use a compact constructor (no parameters) for validation; the assignment is implicit
Override the constructor with a new signature
Add validation to the accessor method instead
questions.explanation: Records support a 'compact constructor' where parameters are omitted and field assignments are implicit. In this form, you only write the validation logic. The compiler automatically adds 'this.celsius = celsius' at the end. This is the cleanest way to add validation to a record without repeating field assignments.
hints: The compact constructor has no parameter list at all
Field assignments happen automatically, so you just write validation

questions.title: Enum Values with Associated Data
questions.description: What is the output of the following Java code?
questions.explanation: Each Planet constant carries its own mass and radius. MARS.surfaceGravity() computes: G * mass / radius^2 = 6.67e-11 * 6.39e23 / (3390^2) ≈ 3.69 m/s^2. The enum provides a clean way to associate data and behavior with each constant. Each constant (EARTH, MARS) has its own mass and radius values set via the constructor.
hints: Each enum constant has its own values for mass and radius
Use Mars' values in the formula: G * M / R^2

questions.title: Record Accessor Methods
questions.description: For a record 'record Person(String name, int age) { }', what are the accessor method names?
options: getName() and getAge()
name() and age()
name and age (direct field access)
get(0) and get(1)
questions.explanation: Records use accessor methods named after the component (not JavaBean getX convention). For record Person(String name, int age), the accessors are name() returning String and age() returning int. This is the same convention as Kotlin data classes. If you prefer JavaBean naming, you can override with getName() and getAge().
hints: Record accessors do NOT follow the JavaBean get/set pattern
The accessor name matches the component name exactly

questions.title: Immutable Data with Records
questions.description: Can you modify a record's field values after creation?
options: Yes, records are mutable by default
No, all record fields are private and final — they cannot be modified after creation
Yes, but only within the same package
No, but you can use reflection to change them
questions.explanation: Record components are implicitly private final fields. Once a record is created, its values cannot be changed. There are no setter methods. This immutability is a core design goal of records — they are meant to be transparent data carriers that are inherently thread-safe and reliable.
hints: The 'final' keyword on fields prevents reassignment
Records are designed to be immutable by default

questions.title: Local Class Accessing Local Variables
questions.description: Which local variables can a local class access?
options: All local variables in the method
Only local variables that are declared as final or are effectively final
Only static local variables
Local classes cannot access local variables
questions.explanation: Local classes can only access local variables that are declared as final or are effectively final (not reassigned after initialization). This is because the local class instance may outlive the method call (if passed elsewhere), and Java creates a copy of the variable in the class. If the variable were reassigned, the copy would not reflect the change, leading to confusing behavior.
hints: The variable must not change after its initial assignment
The technical term for this is 'effectively final'
